newsitem.title: UK: Effects of British Airways strike to drag on.
newsitem.headline: Effects of British Airways strike to drag on.

text.p: British Airways said on Saturday it would be unable to resume normal flights until well into next week because of the spillover effects of a three-day strike by cabin staff.

The 72-hour strike ended early on Saturday but the airline was able to operate only three-quarters of its intercontinental flights from London's Heathrow airport, its main hub, around 45 percent of European services and 40 percent of domestic flights.
British Airways said it expected to operate 85 percent of its long-haul flights from Gatwick airport, south of London.
With crew rosters and aircraft movements badly disrupted by the strike, a similar schedule will operate on Sunday.
By Monday, 85 percent of scheduled long-haul flights from Heathrow should take off, rising to 90 percent on Tuesday, the airline said.
But only 60 percent of European services will operate on those two days from Heathrow, and just over half of domestic British flights.
Gatwick should have returned to normal by Tuesday, according to the airline, which is likely to lose tens of millions of pounds from the strike.

"We are working hard to get our operations back to normal as fast as we can. In the meantime, we are doing our utmost to provide alternative travel arrangements for customers booked on any flights which we cannot operate," the airline said.
Cabin crew went on strike over a plan by the airline to save 42 million pounds ($71 million) and to restructure pay and conditions as part of a drive to sharpen its competitiveness.
BA and the union representing cabin staff have agreed in principle to hold talks to settle the dispute, but a spokeswoman said on Saturday no date had been set for them.

With the busy summer season fast approaching, the airline faces another potential blow on Monday when catering staff decide whether to call their own 24-hour strike in protest at BA's plans to sell its Heathrow catering operations.
